title: 6. 10-Year Financial Forensics, Cash Conversion & Balance Sheet

epigraph.quote: Cash provided by operating activities in 2025 totaled $5,120 million, or 122% of net earnings, up $1 billion compared to 2024.
epigraph.author: General Dynamics Corporation, FY2025 Form 10-K & Earnings Release (January 2026)

web_blocks.html: A ten-year review of General Dynamics (FY2016–FY2025, plus 9M 2026) shows a remarkably steady compounder [1][3][9]. The company absorbed the 2018 CSRA acquisition, navigated the 2020–2021 aviation downturn, and funded heavy shipyard capex. Even so, revenue expanded from $30.56 billion in 2016 to $52.55 billion in 2025 [1][9]. That represents a 6.2% nine-year CAGR, accelerating to 10.1% in 2025 and 10.4% in 9M 2026 [1][3]. Over the same decade, diluted EPS climbed from $9.52 in 2016 to $15.45 in 2025 [9]. Trailing twelve-month EPS reached $17.01 through Q3 2026 [2].

web_blocks.caption: 10-Year Financial Forensics: P&L, Cash Flow & Leverage (FY2016–FY2025)
web_blocks.takeaway: Note: FY2025 Capex is $1,194M per the 2025 Form 10-K ($3,926M FCF). Some third-party aggregators report $1,161M ($3,959M FCF) due to software and lease classification [1][5][9].

web_blocks.html: ROIC vs. WACC & Balance Sheet Deleveraging: General Dynamics posts a trailing 13.22% ROIC and 18.01% ROE. Both sit comfortably above an estimated ~7.5%–8.0% WACC for a defense prime, confirming durable value creation. ROE moderated from ~25%–27% in 2016–2019 to ~17%–18% in 2023–2025, not from weaker margins. Instead, management retained equity to pay down CSRA-era debt [1][9]. Long-term debt fell from $11.40 billion in 2018 to $7.01 billion at year-end 2025 [1][9]. Year-end 2025 also showed $1,006 million in current debt, $2,333 million in cash, and $25,622 million in equity [1]. Net debt of ~$5.68 billion equals ~0.85x trailing EBITDA, leaving ample room for dividends (38.8% payout) and buybacks.

Working Capital & Unbilled Receivables Forensics: Working-capital absorption is the main forensic item on GD's balance sheet. At December 31, 2025, current assets held $2,406 million in billed receivables, $8,380 million in unbilled receivables, and $9,232 million in inventories [1]. Combined unbilled receivables and inventories totaled $17.61 billion, or roughly 33.5% of annual sales. Aerospace inventories naturally liquidate as G700 and G800 deliveries scale. However, the 10-K flags $1.3 billion in net unbilled receivables on one international tracked-vehicle contract in Combat Systems [1]. That balance rose from $1.2 billion in 2024, with billing milestones extending through early 2028 [1]. GD also uses a Master Accounts Receivable Purchase Agreement (MARPA) facility as a standard cash-timing tool [1]. Even so, 2025 CFO of $5,120 million (122% of net earnings) and Q3 2026 CFO of $1.7 billion (139%) confirm strong cash quality [1][2].

Capital Structure, Debt Maturity & Share Count Forensics: Over the past decade, GD steadily de-levered from the 2018 CSRA peak while retiring shares opportunistically [9][11]. By Q3 2026, total debt stood near $7.0 billion against $4.4 billion in cash [12]. Following a $500 million quarterly paydown, net debt dropped to ~$2.6 billion, or ~0.4x EBITDA [12]. Diluted shares fell from ~305 million in FY2016 to ~270.2 million in 2026 [9][11][13]. That reduction boosted per-share EPS and FCF compounding without starving Electric Boat or Gulfstream of capex [9][11][13].

ROIC vs. WACC & Economic Value Creation: Trailing ROIC is 13.22% and ROE is 18.01% against an estimated ~8.5% WACC [13]. That gives GD roughly +470 basis points of positive economic spread above its cost of capital [13]. Crucially, GD achieves this spread with modest leverage (0.33x Debt/Equity) and strong cash backing rather than financial engineering [11][13].

Dividend Coverage & Capital Return Sustainability: GD carries a 38.83% earnings payout ratio ($6.27 TTM dividend) and 6.40% 5-year annual dividend growth [11][13]. Free cash flow covers the dividend more than 2.5x, leaving surplus cash for debt paydown and share buybacks [11][13]. Over FY2016–FY2025, annual free cash flow grew from $1,771 million to $3,926 million [1][9]. Even during the 2020 pandemic year, GD generated $2,891 million in free cash flow [9]. That ten-year cash consistency confirms high earnings quality across both commercial aviation and defense cycles [1][9]. Management has raised the annual dividend consistently while keeping leverage below one turn of EBITDA [9][11][13].

book_paragraphs: Now let's put on our forensic accountant hat and examine ten years of General Dynamics' financial statements from 2016 through 2025. What jumps out first is the sheer steadiness of the compounding engine. Revenue grew from $30.56 billion in 2016 to $52.55 billion in 2025, while diluted EPS rose from $9.52 to $15.45—and hit $17.01 trailing twelve months through Q3 2026. Even during the 2020 pandemic shock, operating income only dipped modestly from $4.57 billion to $4.13 billion before marching higher.

Second, look at the balance sheet discipline. In 2018, General Dynamics borrowed heavily to buy CSRA, pushing long-term debt from $4.0 billion to $11.4 billion. Over the next seven years, management systematically paid that debt down to $7.01 billion by December 31, 2025—with $1.01 billion in current maturities and $2.33 billion in cash sitting against $25.62 billion in shareholders' equity. That deliberate deleveraging is the real reason ROE stepped down from ~26% in 2018–2019 to ~18% today: the denominator grew healthier while net debt shrank to less than one turn of EBITDA. Meanwhile, ROIC sits at 13.22%, clearing an estimated 7.5% to 8.0% cost of capital by more than 500 basis points.

Where should a skeptical analyst poke? Right into working capital. At year-end 2025, General Dynamics carried $8,380 million in unbilled receivables—revenue recognized under long-term contract accounting before cash is billed—and $9,232 million in inventories, mostly Gulfstream jets in production. That is $17.6 billion of working capital, or roughly a third of annual sales.

In the 2025 Form 10-K footnotes, we find one specific concentration to watch: $1.3 billion of those unbilled receivables sits on a single large international tracked-vehicle contract in Combat Systems, up from $1.2 billion in 2024, with billing milestones stretching into early 2028. General Dynamics also uses a Master Accounts Receivable Purchase Agreement—known as MARPA—to factor certain receivables. Those are legitimate tools, not red flags, especially when operating cash flow converts at 122% of net earnings in 2025 and 139% in Q3 2026. But as an owner, you want to see both Gulfstream inventory and that $1.3 billion Combat Systems unbilled balance convert cleanly into cash over the next 24 months.

Take a step back and synthesize all six chapters of our price-blind audit. General Dynamics passes our business-quality screen as a durable compounder: it owns irreplaceable nuclear submarine infrastructure, a high-margin Gulfstream duopoly, and a fortress balance sheet, with KPI health rated PASS_WITH_WATCH only because we want to see Marine Systems margins climb back above 8.5% and G400 certification cross the finish line.

Let us finish our forensic audit with the balance sheet, because a clean balance sheet is what lets a defense prime survive supply-chain hiccups without diluting shareholders. After borrowing to buy CSRA in 2018, management systematically paid down debt out of free cash flow. By the end of Q3 2026, GD held $4.4 billion in cash against just $7.0 billion in total debt—a net debt load of roughly $2.6 billion on a business generating nearly $7 billion in annual EBITDA.

That conservative 0.33x debt-to-equity ratio gives General Dynamics enormous strategic flexibility. It can fund $1.2 billion to $1.5 billion in annual capital expenditures for submarine dry docks and Savannah hangars, pay a growing $6.27-per-share dividend (only a 38.8% payout ratio), retire maturing notes in cash, and still buy back shares whenever the stock dips below intrinsic value. On earnings quality, 122% CFO-to-net-income conversion in FY2025 and 139% in Q3 2026 confirm that GD's profits are real cash, not accrual accounting.

When you put all ten years of financial statements side by side, the single most important number on the page is that 13.22% return on invested capital against an 8.5% cost of capital. That +470-basis-point spread tells you that every dollar General Dynamics reinvests into submarine dry docks, Gulfstream completion hangars, and Combat Systems tooling creates genuine economic value.

Even better, management is not juicing that return with reckless debt. With a 0.33x debt-to-equity ratio, 122% FY2025 operating cash flow conversion, and $500 million of debt retired in Q3 2026 alone, the balance sheet is built to weather both defense-budget squabbles and commercial aviation slowdowns.

For long-term investors, that 38.83% payout ratio is quietly one of the most attractive features in the entire 10-year ledger. General Dynamics has grown its dividend at roughly 6.4% annually over the past five years without ever stretching its balance sheet. Because free cash flow covers the dividend more than two-and-a-half times over, the company can keep raising its payout through recessions while simultaneously paying down debt and shrinking the share count.

In short, the 10-year forensic ledger confirms that General Dynamics' earnings are backed by real cash, conservative leverage, and a +470-basis-point ROIC spread over its cost of capital—precisely the profile we look for in a long-term compounder.

This combination of 122% free cash flow conversion, 0.33x debt-to-equity, and a 38.8% dividend payout ratio gives General Dynamics one of the most durable balance sheets in the entire S&P 500 industrials sector.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Ten-year forensics confirm that General Dynamics is a high-quality industrial compounder, not an accounting mirage. Free cash flow averaged ~$3.4 billion per year from 2020 to 2025 even while funding $1 billion/year in capex, and 122%–139% CFO conversion proves earnings are backed by real cash.
